## The ozone layer

The ozone layer is a region of Earth's stratosphere where ozone (O3) is highly concentrated compared with other parts of the atmosphere, though still small in relation to other gases there.[1]{c1} It lies mainly in the lower stratosphere, roughly 15–35 km above Earth, and even at its peak ozone is dilute — 8 to 15 parts per million in the layer, against about 0.3 parts per million for the atmosphere as a whole.[1]{c2}

The layer's composition is generated from the atmosphere's own oxygen: ozone is created when ultraviolet light strikes ordinary O2 molecules, splitting them into individual oxygen atoms that then combine with unbroken O2.[1]{c3} In turn, the layer changes how the atmosphere interacts with sunlight, absorbing 97–99% of the Sun's medium-frequency ultraviolet light (about 200–315 nm), which would otherwise potentially damage exposed life near the surface.[1]{c4} Its formation is tied to the atmosphere's oxygen history: the ozone layer formed about 500 million years ago, when the Neoproterozoic oxygenation event brought the fraction of oxygen in the atmosphere to about 20%.[1]{c5}

## Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis relates to atmospheric composition chiefly through oxygen. Oxygenic photosynthesis — the usual meaning of the term, carried out by photopigment-bearing autotrophs such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria — releases oxygen as a byproduct of splitting water.[2]{c6} This is what makes photosynthesis play a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of Earth's atmosphere.[2]{c7} On a planetary scale, cyanobacteria appeared later, and the excess oxygen they produced contributed directly to the oxygenation of the Earth, which rendered the evolution of complex life possible.[2]{c8}

## How the two connect

The link is atmospheric oxygen. Oxygen-producing photosynthesis supplies and maintains the O2 in the air; UV light then converts some of that O2 into stratospheric ozone; and the resulting ozone layer absorbs the ultraviolet radiation that would otherwise harm life at the surface. ## Vitamin D (Source 1)

Vitamin D matters for human health chiefly because it enables the intestines to absorb calcium and phosphate; although called a vitamin, it is technically a fat-soluble secosteroid hormone. It is only conditionally essential in the diet, since adequate UVB exposure lets the skin synthesize cholecalciferol, and for most people skin synthesis contributes more than dietary sources. Its importance is clearest in deficiency: fortification programs in some countries and supplement recommendations are intended to prevent or treat deficiency rickets and osteomalacia.[1]{c1} Investigators have nominally linked many other health conditions to low vitamin D, but the evidence that supplementation benefits people who are already sufficient is as yet unproven.[1]{c2}

## Antimicrobial resistance (Source 2)

Antimicrobial resistance matters because microbes of all kinds — bacteria, viruses, parasites, and fungi — can evolve protection against the drugs used to treat infections, making those infections harder to treat and often requiring costly alternative therapies that may have more severe side effects. Misuse and improper management of antimicrobials are the primary drivers, though resistance can also arise naturally through mutation and the spread of resistant genes. The stakes are high: the WHO estimates bacterial AMR was directly responsible for 1.27 million global deaths in 2019 and contributed to over 4 million deaths in 2021.[2]{c3} WHO and other international bodies warn that AMR could lead to up to 10 million deaths annually by 2050 unless actions are taken.[2]{c4}

## Ozone layer (Source 3)

The ozone layer — a region of the stratosphere, roughly 15–35 km up — matters for the planet because it absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation. Specifically, it absorbs 97 to 99 percent of the Sun's medium-frequency ultraviolet light (about 200–315 nm), which otherwise would potentially damage exposed life forms near the surface.[3]{c5} Its vulnerability became clear in 1985, when atmospheric research revealed it was being depleted by industrial chemicals, mainly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).[3]{c6} Concerns that the resulting UV increase threatened life on Earth, including increased skin cancer in humans and other ecological problems, led to bans on those chemicals, and the latest evidence is that depletion has slowed or stopped.[3]{c7}
